description: MaVionix is an interdisciplinary tech and research team working at the intersection of AI, Data Science, Astrophysics and Space Technology. Our team brings together experience in machine learning, computational astronomy, statistical modelling, robotics, software development and product innovation. We are developing M-COSMOS, an interactive platform leveraging SPHEREx observations to explore celestial objects, detect changes across observation epochs and investigate potential moving objects.
summary:
Blink the Sky: MaVionix COSMOS
Spot what moves in NASA’s infrared sky, by MaVionix COSMOS

Blink the Sky is a public viewer for NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey. Type in a sky position or an object's name, and it pulls every SPHEREx image of that spot from NASA/IPAC's archive. Flip between visits and see what moved. Moving objects are found automatically, checked against JPL's catalogue of known asteroids and comets, and labelled "known" or "unmatched", with evidence you can download. A spectrum tool builds a rough 0.75–5 µm colour profile from repeat visits. A Planet Nine page shows the real orbits behind the hypothesis and what SPHEREx could and could not detect. The tool claims no discovery. Unmatched objects are flagged for independent follow-up. It answers the challenge directly: show how SPHEREx images change over time, for anyone.
details:
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Planet X and SPHEREx

Blink the Sky: MaVionix Cosmos

COSMOS turns six-monthly SPHEREx images into something anyone can explore: pick a spot on the sky, flip between its visits, and see what moved.
Team MaVionix

What it does?

COSMOS makes SPHEREx's all-sky infrared images which are taken every six months easy for anyone to explore even without scientific knowledge. The viewer show every image taken of a selected location with zoom, pan, step, blink, swipe and difference options. When the cursor moves over an image it shows RA/Dec, surface brightness and the wavelength recorded by that pixel. Known asteroids and TNOs predicted by JPL can also be displayed on any visit.
The site has five pages:

Viewer: Enter coordinates or a name to see every SPHEREx visit that covers that location. Compare images using step, blink, swipe or difference modes. JPL-known objects and detected moving objects can also be displayed.

Movers: Find sources at 5σ in each visit, connect them in different visits, match them with JPL SBIdent and show an evidence card for each track. Download the results as a CSV report.

Spectrum: Measure a source with its track in every visit and compare its limited 0.75–5 µm spectrum with example templates.

Planet Nine: Explore real TNO orbits, the idea of orbit clustering, how bright a possible Planet Nine would be compared with SPHEREx's detection limit and a measured completeness curve.

How It Works: Explain the complete data-processing process, data sources and citations, limitations and what the tool does not claim.

Figure 1. The viewer. Visit list with detector and wavelength, step / blink / swipe / difference modes, live RA/Dec, surface brightness and wavelength in the cursor and a circled mover track. Screenshot of the demo sample which the app badges as synthetic.

Cursor read-out formulas (Viewer): The cursor position (x, y) is converted to sky coordinates through the FITS WCS, and the wavelength is read from the WCS-WAVE table at the same pixel:

(RA, Dec) = WCS_celestial(x, y)

λ(x, y) = WCS_WAVE(x, y) [µm]

I(x, y) = IMAGE(x, y) − ZODI(x, y) [MJy/sr]

How it works?

The FastAPI backend gets spectral images from IRSA's SIA service for a selected location. It requests 10-arcminute image cutouts from each Level-2 multi-extension FITS file and reads the IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI and WCS-WAVE data extensions.Difference images are created by aligning one visit's image with another using its WCS before subtracting them.Moving objects are found by detecting sources at 5σ in each visit. The detections are then linked in visits when their movement is physically possible and matched with JPL SBIdent predictions.Spectra are created by measuring the source within a fixed opening in every visit and using the wavelength table to find the corresponding wavelengths.

Figure 2. Processing chain: One cutout from each visit goes by three separate processes: difference images, moving objects and spectra. The boxes with thicker outlines show the final results users can see from each process.

Geometry of a cutout. At 6.15″ per pixel, a 10-arcminute cutout is:

N_pix = (10 × 60″) / 6.15″/pix ≈ 97.6 ≈ 98 pixels per side

Difference image (aligned, background-subtracted). Visit A is resampled onto visit B’s pixel grid using the WCS, then:

(xA, yA) = WCSA⁻¹( WCSB(xB, yB) )
D(xB, yB) = [ IB − ZB ](xB, yB) − [ IA − ZA ](xA, yA)
σD = √( σA² + σB² )

Here I is IMAGE, Z is ZODI and σ² is VARIANCE. Positive D (red) means brighter in visit B; negative D (blue) means brighter in visit A.

What each FITS extension is used for:

IMAGE (surface brightness, MJy/sr): Used to display images, detect sources and measure brightness.

FLAGS (pixel quality bits): If any pixel in the 3×3 area around a detection has a flag, the detection is marked as flagged and given a lower score.

VARIANCE (per-pixel noise): Noise σ is calculated by taking the square root of the median variance. This sets the 5σ detection limit.

ZODI (zodiacal-light model): Subtracted first because it is the main background light at 1–5 µm.

WCS-WAVE (wavelength at each pixel): Used to show the wavelength in the cursor, check wavelength pairs and set the spectrum's x-axis.

Mover detection steps and values used:

Detect: DAOStarFinder finds sources using FWHM 1.6 pixels and a 5σ threshold. It is a standard and easy-to-check method. The PSF is about 1–2 pixels at 6.15″ per pixel.

Reject static sources: If a source is found within 9″ in another visit it is treated as a star or galaxy because it has not moved.

Link: Sources are linked if they are at least 9″ apart and move no faster than 400″ per day with an allowed extension of 27″. These limits cover main-belt asteroid speeds and reject accidental matches between different detectors.

Identify: Each track is checked against JPL SBIdent within 30″, and all visits must agree. The track is labelled as either known or unmatched.Figure 3. Movers page. Each candidate carries its evidence: per-visit thumbnails, positions, signal-to-noise, flags, motion and JPL match. Unmatched means unmatched, not new.

Creative contribution

SPHEREx's filters cover different wavelengths in each detector so the same source is recorded at a different colour during each visit. COSMOS uses this as a useful feature. It gives a warning when two visits have different wavelengths and creates a spectrum using repeated images alone.

Figure 4. Colour changes between visits. The wavelengths and detector bands are taken from the demo sample. The curve shows an example shape and is not a real measurement.

The wavelength-pair rule used when comparing two visits:

A wavelength difference of 0.25 µm or less is considered a good match. It is listed as usable for difference images because stars cancel out clearly and moving objects stand out.

A wavelength difference of more than 0.25 µm triggers a warning and the pair is removed from the clean list. This is because stars leave colour-related marks in the difference image and appear twice.

Figure 5. Difference mode. Red is brighter in visit B, blue is brighter in visit A.

Figure 6. Spectrum page. One point per visit, compared with indicative templates only.

Impact and audience

Students, Citizen scientists and teachers can perform the same type of searches as professional researchers without writing any code. The Planet Nine page explains the hypothesis, the evidence from its orbit and the limits of detecting it. All synthetic data is clearly labelled as synthetic.

Students: Compare survey images by blinking between them and watch how a moving object appears (Viewer).

Citizen scientists: Search for moving objects and read the evidence for each track (Movers).

Educators: Teach the Planet Nine hypothesis, its evidence and what it means when no object is found (Planet Nine and How It Works pages).

Researchers: Check every step and value against the original data and cite the results (How It Works page and CSV report).

Could SPHEREx see Planet Nine?

For the With the default input the planet is 3 magnitudes fainter than what a single SPHEREx visit can detect even though its parallax would cover tens of pixels. Combining multiple visits improves detection by 1–2 magnitudes. The page also measures detection completeness by adding artificial sources to a real image cutout.

Figure 7. Brightness against depth. AB magnitudes, brighter to the left. Depth is the app's approximate per-channel 5σ constant.

The calculator at its default inputs (reflected light, phase angle 0):

  • Inputs: 7 Earth masses, albedo 0.4, distance 600 AU.
  • Radius: 2.65 Earth radii (assumed radius proportional to mass to the power 0.5).
  • Absolute magnitude H: −6.03.
  • Apparent V: 21.75.
  • J (AB), approximate: 21.85, assuming a neutral reflector with J close to V + 0.1.
  • Margin against a depth of 19.0 AB: −2.85 mag. Negative means not detectable in a single visit.
  • Annual parallax: 344″, 56 pixels. Large in pixels but the source is too faint.
  • Orbital motion: around 88″ per year for a circular orbit at that distance.

Figure 8. lanet Nine page: Shows real TNO orbits, the orbit-clustering idea, a calculator and a graph showing how well objects can be detected using the injection–recovery method.

Scientific integrity: The tool never claims to have found Planet X. Tracks that do not match JPL predictions are labelled as unmatched not as new objects. Synthetic data is always labelled "SYNTHETIC DATA, NOT SPHEREx".

Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, httpx.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, custom canvas renderer.
  • Data services: IRSA SIA and cutouts for SPHEREx; JPL SBIdent and SBDB for small bodies.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose.
  • Checks: pytest suite (13 tests, offline) and Playwright browser checks.

Limitations stated in the app

  • 6.15″ pixels: Positions are not very exact and point sources cover 1–2 pixels. 4× nearest-neighbour upscaling keeps individual pixels visible without adding any new details.
  • Revisits every six months except near the ecliptic poles: Most areas have only a few visits. Each visit is listed with its date, detector and wavelength.
  • Relative brightness measurements with no opening correction: The spectrum shape is approximate so it is labelled "indicative template comparison" not a classification.
  • Straight-line track linking: Curved or fast-moving objects may be missed. This limitation is clearly mentioned.
  • Synthetic offline sample: The sample does not show real sky observations and is always labelled as synthetic.

Data credits

SPHEREx data: NASA/JPL-Caltech/IPAC, served by the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (QR3 DOI 10.26131/IRSA662, DR1 DOI 10.26131/IRSA678). Small-body data: JPL Solar System Dynamics. This product makes use of data from the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), a joint project of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the California Institute of Technology, funded by NASA.
